1	Lupus tends to appear in women of childbearing age. It can affect pregnancy, however most women with
     2	lupus are able to have children. All pregnancies will need careful medical monitoring because of the
     3	risk of complications. It’s generally best to wait six months after a flare of symptoms and ideally
     4	have no active lupus symptoms prior to conception.
     5	
     6	
     7	 How lupus affects pregnancy
     8	 Lupus is a chronic condition that results from a malfunctioning immune system.
     9	
    10	
    11	 The immune system is designed to identify foreign bodies (such as bacteria and viruses) and attack
    12	them to keep us healthy. However, in the case of lupus, your immune system mistakenly attacks one or
    13	many different types of tissue in the body, such as the skin, joints, muscles, nerves, kidneys,
    14	heart or lungs. The result of this damage is ongoing inflammation and pain.
    15	
    16	
    17	 For these reasons, it’s important that you plan your pregnancy carefully.
    18	
    19	
    20	 The healthier you are before you get pregnant, the greater the chance that you will have a healthy
    21	pregnancy and a healthy baby. Aim to have your condition under control and be in the best possible
    22	health.
    23	
    24	
    25	 Talk with your doctor and specialist before you get pregnant. They may need to make important
    26	changes to your medication to ensure a safe pregnancy. Some medications are safe to take while
    27	you’re pregnant however others, like methotrexate, shouldn’t be taken. You may need to stop taking
    28	some medications months before trying to get pregnant as they can be harmful to your baby. Your
    29	doctors will help you plan this.
    30	
    31	
    32	 In some cases, there is a reduction in lupus symptoms during pregnancy. Your lupus is more likely
    33	to be stable throughout your pregnancy if your condition was stable before conceiving.
    34	
    35	
    36	 Complications of pregnancy
    37	 Most women with lupus are able to have a healthy baby, however sometimes complications can occur.
    38	That’s why it’s so important you plan your pregnancy and work closely with your healthcare team to
    39	ensure you’re as healthy as possible before, during and after your pregnancy.
    40	
    41	
    42	 It’s also important that you know the possible problems that may occur so that you can be treated
    43	immediately. Many of these issues can be prevented or treated effectively if they’re dealt with
    44	early. Some of the problems that can occur during pregnancy for women with lupus include:
    45	
    46	
    47	 flares of your lupus symptoms may occur during pregnancy or immediately after you deliver, however
    48	this is less likely if your condition was stable before you became pregnant
    49	 high blood pressure (hypertension)
    50	 your baby may be born with low birth weight
    51	 pre-eclampsia – symptoms include high blood pressure and excessive amounts of protein lost through
    52	your urine
    53	 premature labour
    54	 increased risk of blood clots in the legs or lungs
    55	 increased risk of miscarriage
    56	 increased risk of emergency caesarean section
    57	 increased risk of excessive bleeding after delivery.
    58	 Medical care before and during pregnancy
    59	 It’s important that you have consistent and adequate medical care before and during your pregnancy.
    60	Discuss your plans to become pregnant with your doctor and specialist before you conceive. They can
    61	advise you of the best time to fall pregnant – it’s advisable to have had no lupus symptoms for at
    62	least six months prior to conception. They can also let you know about any particular risks you may
    63	face and whether your medication needs to be changed. Some medication taken for lupus can cross the
    64	placenta and pose a threat to your baby.
    65	
    66	
    67	 Once you have become pregnant, it's vital that you receive proper antenatal care to anticipate,
    68	prevent and solve any problems that may occur. You will need to contact your treating doctor in case
    69	your treatment needs to be changed or further tests are required.
    70	
    71	
    72	 It’s also important that you consult closely with both a rheumatologist and a specialist
    73	obstetrician throughout your pregnancy to lessen the risk of complications and monitor your baby's
    74	growth.
    75	
    76	
    77	 Lupus flares and normal pregnancy symptoms
    78	 Sometimes, it can be difficult to distinguish between a lupus flare and normal pregnancy symptoms.
    79	For this reason it’s important that you work closely with your healthcare team and obstetrician.
    80	
    81	
    82	 Some of the symptoms of pregnancy that may mimic those of lupus include:
    83	
    84	
    85	 fatigue
    86	 build-up of fluid in the joints
    87	 skin changes, such as rashes, flushes or darkening
    88	 hair loss following childbirth
    89	 shortness of breath
    90	 joint pain.
    91	 Lupus pregnancies and increased rate of premature birth and miscarriage
    92	 During pregnancy, the growing baby is nourished by the placenta. About one third of women with
    93	lupus have antibodies that may cause blood clots and interfere with the proper functioning of the
    94	placenta.
    95	
    96	
    97	 This is most likely to happen in the second trimester. The placenta isn’t able to supply the baby
    98	with sufficient nourishment and the baby’s growth is slowed. This may require early delivery via
    99	caesarean section. If the baby is born after 30 weeks’ gestation, or is at least 1.3 kg in weight,
   100	its chances of survival are good.
   101	
   102	
   103	 Your doctor can screen for antiphospholipid antibodies, and if they are found, may prescribe a
   104	blood thinner to help prevent blood clots. This can help prevent miscarriage in many women.
   105	
   106	
   107	 Pre-eclampsia is a condition that involves increased blood pressure, fluid retention and protein in
   108	the urine. It occurs in one in five women with lupus. If left untreated it can endanger the life of
   109	both the woman and her baby. Pre-eclampsia can be treated. However, depending on the severity, it
   110	may also require early delivery.
   111	
   112	
   113	 Neonatal lupus
   114	 Around one third of women with lupus have antibodies that may cause lupus-like symptoms in their
   115	baby once it‘s born. This is known as neonatal lupus. Symptoms may include skin rash, unusual blood
   116	count and, rarely, heartbeat irregularities. This is not SLE.
   117	
   118	
   119	 In babies who don’t experience heartbeat irregularities, all symptoms of neonatal lupus usually
   120	resolve by three to six months of age. Heartbeat irregularities can be successfully treated.
   121	
   122	
   123	 Lupus and pregnancy delay advice
   124	 Some women with lupus should delay pregnancy and discuss their plan with their treating doctor when
   125	they are planning to have a baby.
   126	
   127	
   128	 They include:
   129	
   130	
   131	 women whose lupus is active
   132	 women taking medication such as methotrexate, mycophenolate, or cyclophosphamide
   133	 women with kidney disease
   134	 women with previous thrombosis or miscarriage.
   135	 If you have any questions about your condition, medications and pregnancy, talk with your doctor.
   136	
   137	
   138	 Where to get help
   139	 Your GP (doctor)
   140	 Obstetrician
   141	 A specialist (often a rheumatologist, nephrologist, immunologist or dermatologist)

Based on `doc.txt`, here is why lupus (an autoimmune disease) complicates healthy pregnancies and healthy babies:

**The underlying problem**
- Lupus is a chronic condition caused by a malfunctioning immune system. Instead of only attacking foreign bodies like bacteria and viruses, the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues — such as skin, joints, muscles, nerves, kidneys, heart, or lungs — causing ongoing inflammation and pain. Because of this, pregnancy needs careful planning and monitoring.

**Complications that can occur during pregnancy**
The document lists several problems that can arise:
- Flares of lupus symptoms during pregnancy or immediately after delivery (less likely if the condition was stable before conception)
- High blood pressure (hypertension)
- Pre-eclampsia — high blood pressure with excessive protein lost through urine. It occurs in one in five women with lupus and, if left untreated, can endanger the life of both the woman and her baby
- Premature labour
- Increased risk of blood clots in the legs or lungs
- Increased risk of miscarriage
- Increased risk of emergency caesarean section
- Increased risk of excessive bleeding after delivery
- The baby may be born with low birth weight

**Placenta problems and premature birth**
- About one third of women with lupus have antibodies that may cause blood clots and interfere with the proper functioning of the placenta, most likely in the second trimester. The placenta then can't supply the baby with sufficient nourishment, the baby's growth is slowed, and early delivery via caesarean section may be required. Doctors can screen for these (antiphospholipid) antibodies and prescribe a blood thinner, which can help prevent miscarriage in many women.

**Risks to the baby after birth (neonatal lupus)**
- Around one third of women with lupus have antibodies that may cause lupus-like symptoms in their baby once it's born — skin rash, unusual blood count, and rarely heartbeat irregularities. (Symptoms usually resolve by three to six months, and heartbeat irregularities can be treated.)

**Medication issues**
- Some lupus medications, like methotrexate, shouldn't be taken during pregnancy and can be harmful to the baby; some medication can cross the placenta and pose a threat to the baby. Women may need to stop certain medications months before trying to conceive, and doctors may need to change treatment.

**Diagnosis difficulties**
- It can be hard to distinguish a lupus flare from normal pregnancy symptoms, since pregnancy can cause fatigue, fluid build-up in the joints, skin changes (rashes, flushes, darkening), hair loss after childbirth, shortness of breath, and joint pain — all of which can mimic lupus.

**Who should delay pregnancy**
- Women whose lupus is active, women taking medications such as methotrexate, mycophenolate, or cyclophosphamide, women with kidney disease, and women with previous thrombosis or miscarriage are advised to delay pregnancy and discuss plans with their doctor.

The document notes that despite these complications, most women with lupus are able to have a healthy baby — the healthier and more stable the woman is before conception (ideally no active symptoms for at least six months), and the closer she works with her healthcare team (rheumatologist and specialist obstetrician), the better the chances of a healthy pregnancy and baby.
